source_review.notes: Checked current official Linux kernel documentation for deadline scheduling, real-time group bandwidth, PREEMPT_RT theory and differences, osnoise, timerlat, hardware-latency detection and rt-mutex design, plus Linux man-pages for scheduling, deadline attributes and absolute sleeps. All eleven primary URLs returned HTTP 200. Kernel mechanisms, conditional scheduling results, measurement guidance and engineering recommendations remain separately scoped.

evidence: Checked release, execution, deadline, period, jitter, blocking, response-time, higher-priority-set and utilization notation.
Verified the fixed-priority recurrence uses a ceiling for higher-priority releases and distinguishes relative from absolute deadlines.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Symbols are defined before analytical use, units are consistent in the worked task set, and the chapter does not conflate wakeup latency, response time or end-to-end latency.

evidence: Recomputed response bounds A=1, B=2 and C iterations 3, 5, 6, 7, 7; all are no greater than deadlines 4, 5 and 10.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The deterministic Python snippet reproduced every displayed result and reports schedulability only for the explicitly stated one-processor task model.

evidence: Re-derived the response-time recurrence from own execution, bounded lower-priority blocking and repeated higher-priority interference within the response window.
Checked that convergence within D is a conditional schedulability conclusion and that divergence beyond D is failure under the same model.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The derivation depends on independent sporadic tasks, fixed priorities, compatible preemption, bounded demand and modeled jitter and blocking; no broader theorem is claimed.

evidence: Reviewed overload, budget depletion, deadline miss, zero recovery bandwidth, interrupt storms, nested inversion, page faults, I/O timeout, thermal throttling and virtual-CPU steal.
Reviewed unmodeled firmware latency, trace loss, observer effect, release bursts, shared-cache interference, stale results and privileged denial of service.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Scheduler, synchronization, kernel, memory, device, multicore, virtualization, energy, observability and recovery boundaries receive distinct treatment.

evidence: Traced each admitted activity from event release and bounded demand through priority or reservation, blocking, execution, useful completion and miss handling.
Verified aggregate admission, complete demand charging, bounded inversion, platform-state control, overload containment and administrative recovery capacity.
invariant_checking.notes: The invariant set joins analysis, enforcement and observation without assuming that any one of them validates the others.

evidence: Reviewed fifteen requirement, task, arrival, demand, resource, policy, blocking, schedulability, admission, enforcement, platform, recovery, observation, change and residual-risk obligations.
Constructed counterexamples for priority-as-guarantee, utilization-as-universal-proof, measured-maximum-as-WCET, PREEMPT_RT-as-total-preemption and isolated-CPU-as-exclusive claims.
proof_review.notes: The chapter offers conditional analysis and assurance obligations, not a formal proof of Linux, arbitrary workloads, platform WCET or universal multicore schedulability.

evidence: Audited uses of guarantee, bound, WCET, sufficient, admission, isolated, worst, hard, feasible and schedulable.
Confirmed analytical assumptions, kernel semantics, empirical observations, engineering policy and unsupported residual latency are labeled separately.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Finite tests are never presented as upper-bound proofs, and the toy recurrence is explicitly limited to its declared scheduling model.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/OS-097/report.json records source, expected and actual output, stderr, exit status, Python toolchain and environment for the response-time example.
Reviewed required release, execution, blocking, interrupt, affinity, bandwidth, clock, fault, thermal, virtualization, trace-loss, overrun and miss evidence.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The passing snippet establishes four arithmetic outputs only; it provides no evidence for production WCET, interrupt bounds, kernel admission, isolation, device latency or a hard real-time platform.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed real-time scheduling as a temporal contract joining task models, conditional feasibility analysis, reservation, bounded blocking, platform interference, overload containment and change control.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed implementable concerns including FIFO/RR and deadline semantics, runtime admission, RT bandwidth, PREEMPT_RT, IRQ placement, CPU isolation, memory residency, I/O, absolute clocks, multicore, virtualization, thermal state, tracing and recovery. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from consequence and task modeling through policy and response-time analysis to platform engineering, overload, evidence and governance, followed by fifteen obligations, fifteen trade-offs, twenty-six misconceptions, ten examples and five complete exercises.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external real-time systems academic, Linux scheduler or PREEMPT_RT maintainer, WCET analyst, safety engineer, embedded practitioner, hardware or firmware expert, independent-verification or certification review is claimed.
